d: An iron meteorite blasted this 1.2 km crater in Arizona about 50,000 years ago, when the climate there was cooler and wetter.
A salty lake in a meteorite crater in India. Luminescence dating gives about 52,000 years; an argon date of about 570,000 years is disputed.
Nine meteorite craters on Saaremaa, Estonia, most likely made shortly after 1530–1450 BCE; age estimates still vary widely.
The caldera lake left by the Toba supereruption about 74,000 years ago, the largest known explosive eruption of the last 25 million years.
A crater lake in Germany’s Eifel formed by a large eruption about 13,000 years ago (12,880 or 13,006 years, depending on the dating method).
A huge Ice Age lake in Utah, formed about 30,000 years ago and shrunk to the Great Salt Lake by about 13,000 years ago.
About 17,400 years ago Lake Bonneville broke through Red Rock Pass, Idaho, releasing about 5,000 km³ of water down the Snake River.
An ice-dammed lake in Montana that filled and burst again and again between about 15,000 and 13,000 years ago.
Bare, gouged land in eastern Washington carved by dozens of Ice Age floods from Lake Missoula, roughly 18,000 to 13,000 years ago.
The falls began at the Niagara Escarpment near Queenston about 10,900 years ago and have since eaten about 11 km upstream.
A large meltwater lake over the upper Great Lakes basins from about 12,000 years ago, replaced about 7,000 years ago as the ice retreated.
A meltwater lake larger than today’s Lake Ontario, about 13,000 years ago.
An arm of the Atlantic that flooded the ice-depressed St Lawrence and Ottawa valleys from about 13,000 to 10,000 years ago.
An Ice Age lake in Nevada, over 22,000 km² at its peak about 12,700 years ago and largely gone by about 9,000 years ago.
The Ice Age forerunner of the Dead Sea, filling the Jordan Valley up to about 200 m above today’s level. It fell sharply around 14,000–13,000 BCE (start date approximate).
Africa’s largest lake dried out completely about 17,300 years ago and refilled about 14,700 years ago as the African Humid Period began.
Huge undersea landslides off Norway around 6200 BCE sent a tsunami across the North Atlantic, reaching up to 29 km inland in Scotland.
A brackish stage of the Baltic Sea, about 8,500 to 4,000 years ago, when salt water flowed in through the Danish straits.
Mount Mazama collapsed in a huge eruption about 7,700 years ago; its caldera filled to become Crater Lake, the deepest lake in the US.
A caldera west of Naples shaped by the Campanian Ignimbrite eruption about 39,300 years ago, and reshaped by the Neapolitan Yellow Tuff eruption roughly 15,000–12,000 years ago (dates vary).
The Somma volcano formed over 25,000 years ago (estimate); Vesuvius grew inside its collapsed caldera.
The youngest volcano of the Carpathians had explosive eruptions between about 56,000 and 32,000 years ago; its last eruption was 32,600–27,500 years ago.
A caldera lake in Kamchatka formed by a very large eruption in 6460–6414 BCE that spread ash up to 1,700 km away.
A mostly underwater caldera off Kyushu. Its Akahoya eruption 7,300–7,200 years ago was one of the largest of the Holocene.
The caldera at the head of Kagoshima Bay, formed by huge eruptions about 30,000 years ago; Sakurajima volcano grows inside it.
New Zealand’s largest lake fills a caldera made by the Oruanui supereruption about 25,600 years ago.
Five small meteorite craters in Yakutia, Siberia, probably made around 5300 BCE (estimate; coordinates approximate).
A dozen craters in central Australia made when an iron meteorite broke up; dated to about 4,700–4,200 years ago.
Meteorite craters in the Empty Quarter of Arabia. One study suggests they are under 250 years old; an older estimate is about 6,400 years (debated).
The youngest volcano of Hawaiʻi’s Big Island grew above sea level about 100,000 years ago; 90% of its surface is lava under 1,000 years old.
"Child of Krakatoa" first rose from the sea on 29 December 1927, in the caldera left by the 1883 eruption.
A volcano that rose from a Mexican cornfield in 1943 and erupted until 1952.
A new volcanic island off Iceland, born in an eruption from November 1963 to 1967; a living lab for how life colonises new land.
A new volcanic cone on Heimaey, Iceland, formed in the 1973 eruption that buried part of the town.
The eruption of 18 May 1980 blew away the volcano’s north side, leaving a horseshoe-shaped crater.
The world’s largest permafrost thaw slump in Yakutia, about 1 km long and up to 100 m deep. It began sinking in the 1960s after forest clearing and still grows; Ice Age fossils fall out of its walls.
A fissure eruption from August 2014 to 2015 laid down over 85 km² of new lava, Iceland’s largest since 1783.
An eruption joined two Tongan islets into one in 2015; the huge January 2022 eruption split them again.
Once the world’s third-largest lake, it began shrinking in the 1960s after Soviet irrigation diverted its rivers; by 2007 it was 10% of its former size.
A huge forest elephant of Europe in warm periods. Youngest secure remains, from Iberia, are about 44,000 years old (possibly younger).
A large European hippo that ranged across Europe until about 400,000 years ago.
The largest ape ever, known from teeth and jaws in southern China caves; it died out about 295,000–215,000 years ago as its forests shrank.
A giant straight-tusked elephant of the Indian subcontinent. It vanished within the last 50,000 years, possibly as late as 25,000 years ago (uncertain).
Elephants shrank on Sicily and Malta; the tiny P. falconeri lived from at least 500,000 years ago, and a later dwarf species survived to about 20,000 years ago.
The "Siberian unicorn", a giant one-horned rhino of the steppe. It survived in southern Russia until at least 39,000, possibly 35,000, years ago.
A large hyena that denned in caves across Eurasia. The youngest well-dated European remains are about 31,000 years old (possibly 24,000).
The scimitar-toothed cat, rarer in Eurasia after the Middle Pleistocene; in North America it lasted until about 12,000 years ago.
Arctodus simus, one of the largest land carnivores of Ice Age North America, died out about 12,800 years ago.
Castoroides, a bear-sized beaver of North American wetlands, first found in an Ohio bog in 1837; extinct about 11,000 years ago.
A long-necked, camel-like hoofed animal of South America, first found by Darwin; extinct about 12,000 years ago.
A rhino-sized South American hoofed mammal, among the fossils Darwin collected; extinct about 12,000 years ago.
A car-sized armoured relative of armadillos in South America, extinct around 12,000–11,000 years ago.
A glyptodont with a spiked club tail; possibly the last glyptodont, with debated remains as young as 8,000–7,000 years.
A giant monitor lizard of Australia; the youngest possible remains, from Mount Etna Caves in Queensland, are about 50,000 years old.
The "marsupial lion", Australia’s top mammal predator, extinct about 40,000 years ago.
A heavy flightless bird of Australia, the last of the "thunder birds", extinct about 50,000–40,000 years ago.
A giant short-faced kangaroo, present until at least 45,000 years ago (possibly until 18,000).
A flightless North Atlantic seabird that appeared about 400,000 years ago; the last confirmed pair was killed on Eldey, Iceland, in June 1844.
The largest known eagle, which hunted moa on New Zealand’s South Island; extinct around 1445 after the moa disappeared.
Giant flightless birds of Madagascar that laid the largest known eggs; extinct around 1000 CE, probably through human activity.
Pygmy hippos of Madagascar; fossils show at least one species lived until about 1,000–400 years ago, perhaps later (uncertain).
Asphalt seeps in Los Angeles that trapped Ice Age animals; the oldest dated material is about 38,000 years old, and the seeps are still active.
A sinkhole pond in South Dakota that trapped dozens of mammoths. A 2026 study dates it to about 232,000–160,000 years ago (older estimates: about 26,000).
A nursery herd of at least 19 Columbian mammoths drowned in a flash flood about 68,000 years ago, with more victims about 15,000 years later.
A lake bed at Snowmass, Colorado, packed with mastodons, mammoths and other animals from about 140,000 to 77,000 years ago.
Fossils of mammoths, camels, ground sloths, dire wolves and American lions near Las Vegas, about 250,000 to 7,000 years old.
w: Tule Springs Fossil Beds National Monument

d: A Devon cave with handaxes and Ice Age bones in layers from about 478,000 to 30,000 years ago.
Wooden throwing spears found with butchered horses, among the oldest hunting weapons known. Dated about 337,000–300,000 years ago (other estimates: 400,000 or 200,000).
Cave pitfall traps in South Australia holding a long record of Ice Age megafauna; World Heritage site since 1994.
The best-preserved mammoth carcass ever found, a young mammoth from the Laptev Sea coast found in 2010; radiocarbon age 34,300 years (about 39,000 calendar years, estimate).
A month-old mammoth calf that died about 42,000 years ago, found almost intact by a reindeer herder on the Yuribey River, Yamal, in 2007 (coordinates approximate).
A mammoth found on the Taymyr Peninsula in 1997 and airlifted in a 23-tonne block of frozen ground; it lived about 20,000 years ago.
A Patagonian cave where skin and dung of the ground sloth Mylodon were found in 1895; the animal died 13,560–10,200 years ago (coordinates approximate).
A Venezuelan site where a mastodon pelvis was found pierced by a stone point, dated to about 13,000 years ago (coordinates approximate).
A Chilean campsite where people ate gomphotheres about 14,500 years ago, before Clovis; a 2026 paper argues it is far younger (debated).
Yukon caves with butchered animal bones suggesting people were in Beringia about 24,000 years ago (contested).
Seeds of Silene stenophylla stored by ground squirrels on the Kolyma about 32,000 years ago were grown into living plants in 2012 (location approximate).
A single clonal quaking aspen in Utah whose stems share one root system. Its age is estimated at 9,000–16,000 years; the popular figure of 80,000 is outdated.
A Norway spruce in Sweden whose root system is about 9,550 years old (carbon dating); the visible trunk is much younger.
A Great Basin bristlecone pine at least 4,862 years old, cut down in 1964 for study.
A yew in a Welsh churchyard said to be 4,000–5,000 years old; other estimates are about 1,500 years (uncertain).
The oldest giant cedar on Yakushima, Japan; at least 2,000 years old, with estimates up to 7,200 years.
The largest living tree by volume, a giant sequoia in California about 2,300–2,700 years old.
